Most office and retail buildings run their heating and cooling on schedules programmed years ago, and nobody has retold the building management system since. Gridmaple's framing of the problem is concrete: at 6 a.m. a tower is already conditioning for a workforce that, post-hybrid, arrives unevenly at 9:30 and mostly on floors 4 through 11. The BMS is doing exactly what it was told in 2016, and the controls contractor charges by the visit to change it. HVAC is typically the largest energy load in these buildings, and static schedules leave money on the table through empty-floor conditioning, pre-cooling on mild days, and zones fighting each other.

Gridmaple attacks this without new hardware. Its software connects to the existing BMS over BACnet — the protocol the building already speaks — and works with major platforms including Johnson Controls Metasys, Siemens Desigo, and Honeywell. There are no sensors to install and no retrofit; onboarding is a points-mapping exercise rather than a construction project, with the team mapping zones, air handlers, and setpoints in the first two weeks using as-built documentation where it exists and discovery where it does not. A single site appliance is racked only where the BMS has no network route.

From there, machine-learning models trained on the building's own history forecast occupancy and weather for each zone and compute optimized schedules and setpoints every 15 minutes. Occupancy signals can come from badge data or network activity, or from learned patterns where those are absent. The models also learn thermal response — how fast a particular floor warms, how long the chilled water loop takes to answer — so they can start equipment later on slow days, pre-cool less when the afternoon will be mild, and stagger equipment starts to avoid demand spikes. Changes flow back to the BMS inside guardrails the facilities team defines: temperature bands per zone, cycling limits, blackout periods, and untouchable floors or systems. Every adjustment is logged with its reason and is reversible with one click, and operators get a daily digest of what changed and why.

The product optimizes against dollars rather than kilowatt-hours alone. Gridmaple loads the customer's tariff — time-of-use windows, demand-charge structure, seasonal rates — and shifts load away from peak windows. Where utilities run demand-response programs, it can absorb events by pre-conditioning ahead of the window and floating through it inside the comfort band, with an event log as proof of performance. The site is blunt about why this matters: energy bills are two meters, consumption and peak demand, and the demand half is the one nobody optimizes.

Savings claims in this industry have a credibility problem, and Gridmaple's answer is measurement against the utility meter, weather-normalized, using industry-standard M&V practice with the building's own metered history as the baseline. The company reports that customers measure 15 to 30 percent savings on HVAC. The same data package supports utility rebate applications — several customers fund part of their subscription through efficiency programs — and feeds emissions disclosures with per-building, per-month figures. Utility program managers in three states accept the M&V package as rebate documentation without supplemental metering.

The customer base is owners and operators of office, retail, and healthcare portfolios, from a single 80,000-square-foot building to portfolios of 200 sites, with municipal and university estates a growing segment. Use cases differ by type: office landlords use it to hit lease energy targets and answer tenant sustainability questionnaires with metered data; retail portfolios standardize one optimization layer across hundreds of nearly identical sites with no on-premise facilities staff; healthcare operators run it on administrative and outpatient buildings with clinical spaces excluded by guardrail. The retail case is the clearest pattern — remote-first BACnet connection, points mapping templated from the prototype store design, observe mode across the whole estate at once, then optimization switched on in cohorts with M&V rolled up per region and per banner.

Pricing is per building per year, sized by floor area, inclusive of onboarding, M&V reporting, and rate-tariff updates. The company explicitly avoids percentage-of-savings contracts and shared-savings accounting disputes, offering a flat price an asset manager can budget. Deployment runs on a stated timeline: weeks one and two for BACnet connection and points mapping, weeks three and four in observe mode where models learn but do not write, and closed-loop optimization from week five, with full savings ramping within the first quarter as the models see a season change.

Gridmaple is headquartered in New York City, founded in 2021 by controls engineers and a former utility analyst, and has 52 people across engineering, building science, and customer operations, with field engineers in the metros where its largest portfolios operate. Founders Peter Voss and Miguel Santos spent a combined twenty years programming building controls and watching optimizations decay the day the commissioning engineer left the site; Hannah Cole priced commercial tariffs at a utility. The company describes itself as the product of that overlap — controls depth plus tariff literacy, applied continuously by software instead of occasionally by site visit. On the technology choices it is equally specific: it does not replace the BMS, buildings keep running the last written schedule if the internet drops, operators can always override, and customers own their data and can export it at any time.
